title: Rethinking Multi-View Fusion for Urban Representation Learning

paper.title: Rethinking Multi-View Fusion for Urban Representation Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Urban region representation learning encodes heterogeneous urban signals—such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use patterns—into unified embeddings for downstream tasks, including check-in prediction, crime forecasting, and service demand estimation.
Existing approaches rely on globally shared fusion and joint optimization, implicitly assuming uniform modality importance and naturally balanced multi-objective training.
However, urban data is inherently heterogeneous. Our empirical analysis reveals two structural issues: (i) modality utility varies markedly across regions, causing static fusion to overemphasize signals from certain modalities; and (ii) heterogeneous objectives exhibit persistent gradient imbalance, causing representational bias and unstable training.
We present PRISM , a self-adjusting framework for adaptive multi-view learning. PRISM adapts sparse MoE routing to learn region-specific view allocations, while a PID (Proportional Integral Derivative)-inspired regulation mechanism mitigates gradient conflicts during optimization.
Experiments on three large-scale urban datasets show that PRISM achieves competitive performance than strong multi-view baselines, while providing more stable optimization behavior and more balanced region representations.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Cities are increasingly instrumented with sensing and digital infrastructures that continuously generate heterogeneous data from mobility networks, land-use registries, transportation systems, and socio-economic activities ( Xu et al., 2025a ) . This data provides unprecedented opportunities for understanding urban dynamics. Yet, heterogeneity in terms of structure, granularity, noise ratio, and spatial coverage poses fundamental data integration and computational modeling challenges. Urban region representation learning has emerged as a principled abstraction for addressing these challenges ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2027 ) . Transforming diverse urban signals into compact embeddings enables computational models that capture latent spatial functionality and inter-region relationships in a unified vector form. These embeddings serve as reusable, transferable representations that support a wide range of analytical tasks, including check-in prediction ( Liang and Zhang, 2023 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) , crime forecasting ( Butt et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , traffic modeling ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2021b ; Yang et al., 2022a ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2027 ; Yang et al., 2021a ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2022b ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Yang and Yang, 2020 ) , and service demand estimation ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025a ) . Given the heterogeneous nature of urban data, a central question arises: how should multiple urban signals be integrated to construct reliable region representations? Structured multi-view fusion. Existing approaches treat each urban modality—such as mobility flow graphs, POI distributions, or land-use maps—as an independent structured signal that is encoded using graph or attribute-based models. Representative methods (e.g., MGFN ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , HAFusion ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , CGAP ( Xu and Zhou, 2024 ) ) jointly learn representations from multiple modalities and fuse them by means of concatenation, attention, or weighted aggregation. More recent studies extend this paradigm to cross-modal settings by incorporating additional sources such as street-view images (e.g., FlexiReg ( Sun et al., 2025a ) ). While being architecturally diverse, these methods adopt a shared abstraction: heterogeneous views are integrated via globally shared fusion mechanisms under deterministic parameterization. Multi-objective optimization in multi-view learning. Multi-view urban representation learning typically introduces modality-specific objectives that guide the shared embedding towards distinct structural or semantic properties. These objectives are then jointly optimized within a unified parameter space without explicit coordination. Although general multi-task strategies (e.g., gradient normalization or projection) have been explored in other domains, they assume task symmetry and do not account for the spatially heterogeneous and modality-dependent dynamics intrinsic to urban data. Despite their methodological variations, existing approaches rely on two implicit assumptions: (i) modality importance is spatially consistent across regions , and (ii) joint optimization of heterogeneous objectives naturally produces coordinated and balanced representations . Motivating example. To evaluate these assumptions, we analyze on three city-scale datasets (see Figure 1 ). Figure 1 a highlights task-dependent differences in modality utility: mobility signals are most informative for crime prediction, whereas land-use and POI features are more useful for service call prediction, suggesting differing underlying spatial dynamics. Notably, as highlighted by the red dashed oval, POI and land-use features contribute negligibly to the SF Crime task. This pronounced heterogeneity challenges the assumption of globally uniform fusion across modalities. Figure 1 b further reveals a systematic optimization imbalance under conventional joint training (e.g., the red dashed oval). Gradients associated with different modality-specific objectives exhibit persistent magnitude disparities, allowing dominant modalities to steer the shared embedding space while suppressing weaker yet informative signals. Such imbalance induces representational bias and ultimately degrades cross-region generalization. Figure 1 . Motivation Example on San Francisco Dataset. Following this analysis, we identify two coupled research challenges that remain unresolved in urban region representation learning: Challenge 1 (C1): Spatially adaptive view integration. The predictive utility of each modality is inherently region-dependent, and yet existing fusion mechanisms assign contributions through globally shared parameters. This mismatch between local data characteristics and global fusion strategies incurs representational bias—commercial regions may be well-served while residential regions may be systematically under-represented. The challenge is to enable region-aware, adaptive modality selection that aligns representation capacity with spatial heterogeneity, without requiring region-specific supervision. Challenge 2 (C2): Coordinated optimization under heterogeneous objectives. When multiple modality-specific objectives with different gradient scales, noise levels, and convergence rates are jointly optimized in a shared embedding space, objectives associated with certain modalities may contribute disproportionately large or more stable gradients, causing them to dominate the optimization process and suppress weaker modality signals, which in turn leads to imbalanced representations and unstable training. The challenge is to explicitly regulate the interplay among competing objectives so that all informative modalities contribute proportionally to the final representation. To address the two challenges, we propose PRISM ( P er- R egion I ntegration with S elf-regulating M ulti-view coordination), a unified framework that redefines multi-view urban representation learning as an adaptive coordination problem rather than as a static aggregation procedure. In particular, PRISM builds on an existing multi-view encoding backbone and focuses on two components: region-level sparse view routing and PID-inspired discrepancy regulation. Region-level adaptive routing via sparse MoE. For modeling, PRISM instantiates region-level view allocation with a standard sparse MoE routing design. Our goal is not to introduce a new generic MoE routing operator, but to adapt sparse routing to heterogeneous urban view fusion. Different from token-level MoE routing over homogeneous sequence elements, the routed unit in PRISM is a region-view representation derived from mobility, POI, or land-use signals. The router dynamically selects and prioritizes informative views for each region, enabling localized view specialization while suppressing redundant or noisy signals. This addresses C1 by aligning view contributions with the spatial heterogeneity observed in Figure 1 (a). PID-inspired multi-objective discrepancy regulation. For optimization, PRISM introduces a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer to coordinate heterogeneous view-induced objectives. We borrow the proportional–integral–derivative decomposition to model complementary discrepancy signals during training. Specifically, the proportional term captures the current discrepancy, the integral term captures accumulated bias, and the derivative term captures short-term variation. These terms are used as loss-level regularization penalties rather than as a single control signal acting on the system. This transforms multi-view learning from implicit joint optimization into an explicitly regularized coordination process, addressing the gradient imbalance identified in C2 . In summary, the main contributions are as follows: • Region-Level Adaptive View Allocation. We formulate multi-view urban representation learning as a region-level adaptive view allocation problem, where different regions may rely on different subsets of mobility, POI, and land-use signals. We instantiate this formulation with sparse MoE routing to enable selective view integration at the region granularity. • PID-Inspired Optimization Coordination. We formulate multi-view representation learning as an adaptive optimization coordination problem and introduce a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer that captures current discrepancy, accumulated bias, and local variation. The final loss aggregation adopts uncertainty-based weighting to adaptively balance heterogeneous objectives, while the proposed contribution lies in PID-inspired discrepancy modeling rather than the weighting scheme. This design mitigates gradient conflicts and stabilizes training under heterogeneous view-induced objectives. • Comprehensive Empirical Validation. Extensive experiments on three large-scale urban datasets across multiple downstream tasks evaluate the effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency of PRISM .

sections.heading: 2.1. Urban Region Representation Learning
sections.text: Urban region representation learning aims to derive compact embeddings that encode functional, structural, and interaction patterns of spatial regions. From a data modeling perspective, existing work can be broadly categorized into single-source modeling and heterogeneous multi-source modeling , according to how urban signals are organized and integrated. Single-source approaches learn region embeddings from a dominant urban signal ( Yao et al., 2018 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) , such as mobility flows, POI distributions, or land-use attributes. For example ZE-Mob ( Yao et al., 2018 ) encodes a mobility transition graph using skip-grams. This type of method typically constructs region-level graphs or attribute matrices and apply graph representation learning, random-walk-based embedding, or matrix factorization techniques to obtain compact representations. Some studies extend this paradigm by extracting multiple complementary views from the same modality, e.g., using temporal slicing of mobility flows or structural and semantic similarity graphs, and then aggregate these views, the goal being to enhance robustness ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) . While such designs enrich representations based on a single modality, the learned embeddings remain shaped by the inductive bias and information scope of the specific modality. To increase representational completeness, more recent studies ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023c ; Sun et al., 2025a ) integrate heterogeneous urban signals, including mobility, POIs, land use, socio-economic attributes, and environmental features. These methods seek to capture complementary information from different modalities by constructing multi-graph architectures, cross-attention mechanisms, shared latent spaces, or fusion-based embedding frameworks. Employing joint optimization, they aim to produce unified region representations that reflect multiple aspects of urban dynamics. Modality interactions are typically modeled through feature concatenation or shared attention mechanisms, resulting in a single embedding embodying information from all available views.

sections.heading: 2.2. Mixture-of-Experts and Adaptive Routing
sections.text: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models enable conditional computation by routing inputs to specialized experts through learned gating functions ( Li et al., 2023a ; Nguyen et al., 2024a ) . They have been widely adopted in large-scale neural models to increase model capacity while maintaining computational efficiency ( Nie et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Existing MoE routing strategies mainly differ in sparsity and expert-allocation design. Switch Transformer ( Fedus et al., 2022 ) performs sparse token-level routing by assigning each token to selected feed-forward experts, while GShard ( Lepikhin et al., 2021 ) adopts top- k k routing with auxiliary balancing losses. Expert Choice ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) reverses the assignment direction to improve expert utilization, and Soft MoE ( Puigcerver et al., 2024 ) replaces discrete routing with continuous mixture weights. These methods are primarily developed for homogeneous token streams and emphasize scalability, load balancing, and efficient conditional computation. Recent studies extend MoE to multi-modal and spatio-temporal settings. In multi-modal learning, methods such as MoME ( Shen et al., 2024 ) and VLMo ( Bao et al., 2022 ) activate experts according to modality or layer-level signals. In spatio-temporal forecasting, ST-MoE ( Li et al., 2023b ) routes temporal inputs to specialized experts to capture temporal heterogeneity. MoE has also been explored in urban computing. For example, UrbanMoE ( Liu et al., 2026 ) applies sparse multi-modal expert routing to multi-task urban region profiling, using satellite imagery, textual descriptions, and POI features to predict multiple urban indicators. Different from these studies, PRISM focuses on reusable urban region representation learning from mobility, POI, and land-use views. Its goal is not to introduce a new generic MoE routing operator, but to adapt standard sparse MoE routing to region-level heterogeneous view allocation. In this setting, the routed unit is a region-view representation, and the routing decision determines which urban views should contribute to each region. This differs from token-level routing in large language models, modality-aware routing in multi-modal learning, temporal routing in forecasting, and task-aware expert routing in urban profiling. Recent meta-learning studies further explore spatial adaptation in urban prediction, such as region-adaptive prediction with region profiles and few-shot transfer from data-sufficient cities to data-scarce cities ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) . These methods mainly adapt prediction models under limited observations, whereas PRISM studies region-level coordination among structurally distinct urban views within a unified representation learning framework.

sections.heading: 2.3. Adaptive Multi-Task Learning and PID-Inspired Regulation
sections.text: Adaptive multi-task learning (MTL) jointly optimizes multiple objectives while mitigating task imbalance and gradient interference. Representative methods include GradNorm ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , which balances task training rates through gradient magnitude normalization; PCGrad ( Yu et al., 2020 ) , which projects conflicting gradients; and MGDA ( Désidéri, 2012 ; Sener and Koltun, 2018 ) , which seeks a common descent direction toward Pareto-stationary solutions. These methods mainly operate on instantaneous task gradients and are typically designed for conventional MTL settings with comparable supervised tasks. Several recent studies incorporate PID principles into neural learning systems, but at different levels. PIDformer ( Nguyen et al., 2024b ) introduces a PID closed-loop feedback signal into transformer state-space dynamics to improve robustness and mitigate rank collapse. PID-based stochastic optimization ( An et al., 2018 ) treats gradients as control errors and updates network parameters using current, accumulated, and changing gradient information. Different from these methods, PRISM addresses heterogeneous view-induced objectives in urban representation learning, where mobility models origin–destination interactions, while POI and land-use preserve view-specific similarity structures. PRISM does not apply PID to attention dynamics or optimizer states. Instead, it introduces a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer over view-induced objectives, where the proportional, integral, and derivative terms model current discrepancy, accumulated bias, and short-term variation during training. We further include GradNorm , PCGrad , and MGDA as controlled baselines under the same backbone to empirically examine this distinction. Figure 2 . The PRISM framework. The multi-view encoding block follows the HAFusion -style backbone; PRISM introduces region-level adaptive routing and PID-inspired discrepancy regularization. GT denotes ground truth.

sections.heading: 4. Methodology
sections.text: Figure 2 presents the overall architecture of PRISM . The multi-view encoding component follows the HAFusion -style backbone and is used to encode mobility, POI, and land-use data defined over shared spatial regions. On top of this backbone, PRISM introduces region-level adaptive routing to allocate view contributions for each region. It further incorporates PID-inspired discrepancy regularization to mitigate gradient imbalance and cross-objective conflicts among heterogeneous view-induced objectives.

sections.heading: 4.3. PID-Inspired Discrepancy Regularization
sections.text: While the proposed routing mechanism enables flexible multi-view integration, the resulting optimization process may still suffer from gradient imbalance and oscillatory discrepancy trajectories. Inspired by the proportional–integral–derivative decomposition in control theory, we introduce a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer. We emphasize that this formulation is not a classical PID controller: instead of combining P/I/D terms into a single control signal, it penalizes the squared proportional, accumulated, and differential discrepancies as separate loss components. Thus, PID-MSE should be understood as a loss-level regularization objective rather than a structurally equivalent PID control law.

sections.heading: 5.1. Settings
sections.text: Datasets. Following the study HAFusion ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , we evaluate PRISM on three real-world datasets, including New York City ( NYC ) 1 1 1 https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/ , Chicago ( Chi ) 2 2 2 https://data.cityofchicago.org/ , and San Francisco ( SF ) 3 3 3 https://datasf.org/opendata/ . For each city, we construct region-level features from multiple urban data sources: Spatial regions. Each city is partitioned into regions that serve as basic analytical units. Mobility data. Taxi trajectories are aggregated into region-level origin–destination (OD) matrices, capturing directed inter-region human flows. POIs. POI data is collected from OpenStreetMap 4 4 4 https://www.openstreetmap.org/ . Region representations are derived from aggregated semantic category counts. Land use. Zoning data describes the distribution of land-use categories within each region (11 for NYC, 12 for Chi, and 13 for SF). Urban activity. Crime reports, Foursquare check-ins 5 5 5 https://sites.google.com/site/yangdingqi/home/foursquare-dataset , and service call records are aggregated at the region level and used as downstream prediction targets ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) . Downstream Applications. To evaluate the effectiveness of the learned urban region representations, we consider three representative applications: check-in prediction , crime forecasting , and service call prediction . These tasks capture diverse aspects of urban dynamics, including human activity intensity, public safety patterns, and infrastructure demand. We formulate all tasks as regression problems, where the objective is to predict the aggregated event counts within each region using the learned embeddings as input features. Following existing studies ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , we employ Lasso regression ( Kumar et al., 2023 ) due to its robustness to high-dimensional features and its ability to mitigate overfitting through sparsity-inducing regularization. sections.heading: 5.2. Overall Performance
sections.text: Check-in Prediction. We begin by evaluating all methods on the check-in prediction task, which measures a model’s ability to capture latent urban functionality and mobility dynamics. As can be seen in Table 1 , PRISM achieves the best performance across all three cities, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline, HAF , on every evaluation metric. In NYC, PRISM reduces the MAE from 202.8 to 200.7 and improves the R 2 R^{2} from 0.844 to 0.852. Similar improvements are observed in both Chi and SF, where PRISM achieves the lowest prediction errors and the highest explanatory power. These results indicate that PRISM more effectively models cross-region interactions and heterogeneous urban signals, which are essential for capturing complex check-in behaviors. Unlike existing baselines that focus on urban region representation learning, multi-task objective optimization, or spatio-temporal dependency modeling, PRISM jointly captures heterogeneous urban semantics, cross-region relational structures, and task-level interactions, thereby producing more discriminative and transferable region embeddings. Crime Forecasting. Next, crime forecasting requires modeling subtle spatial dependencies and socio-environmental factors. As shown in Table 1 , PRISM again delivers the strongest results across all datasets, achieving the lowest MAE and RMSE values while obtaining the highest R 2 R^{2} values. Relative to HAF , PRISM improves R 2 R^{2} from 0.734 to 0.756 in NYC and from 0.631 to 0.668 in Chi, indicating enhanced predictive capability in explaining crime variability. The moderate performance gains are expected, given the inherently stochastic nature of crime data. The results suggest that PRISM learns region embeddings that preserve fine-grained spatial semantics well, thereby supporting more accurate modeling of localized crime patterns. Service Call Prediction. Finally, service call prediction is challenging due to high demand volatility and weak spatial regularity. Here, PRISM achieves the best performance across all cities. For example, in Chi, PRISM improves R 2 R^{2} from 0.613 to 0.650, representing a meaningful relative gain. Comparable improvements are observed in SF, where PRISM surpasses the second-best method across all metrics. The larger performance gap observed for this task suggests that PRISM is particularly effective in complex prediction settings, where robust representation learning is critical. This finding implies that PRISM captures deep structural dependencies rather than shallow correlations.

sections.heading: 5.3. Ablation Studies
sections.text: Table 2 reports the ablation results of PRISM . Overall, the full model achieves strong performance across most settings, but the contribution of each component varies by city and task. Effect of Region-Aware Routing (RAR). Replacing region-aware routing with simple feature concatenation ( w/o RAR ) results in the most consistent performance drop across nearly all settings. The degradation is particularly evident for the check-in task, where R 2 R^{2} decreases from 0.852 0.852 to 0.836 0.836 in NYC and from 0.904 0.904 to 0.850 0.850 in Chi. This confirms that static concatenation tends to entangle heterogeneous signals and cannot adapt to region-specific informativeness. In contrast, region-aware routing prioritizes the most informative views for each region dynamically, enabling the learned embeddings to capture functional heterogeneity better. Similar trends observed for crime and service call prediction further suggest that adaptive routing offers a general advantage rather than being task-specific. Effect of Uncertainty Weighting (UM). Removing uncertainty-based weighting and assigning equal importance to all objectives ( w/o UM ) yields both lower accuracy and higher variance. For example, for check-in prediction in NYC, the MAE increases to 210.3 210.3 with substantially larger variance compared to the full model. This behavior indicates less stable optimization dynamics. Since urban representation learning relies on multiple supervisory signals derived from different modalities, naïvely combining them with fixed weights can introduce gradient conflicts and bias the model toward particular objectives. Uncertainty weighting mitigates this issue by automatically balancing loss contributions, thereby improving convergence stability and cross-city generalization. Effect of PID-MSE (Feedback-Regulated Error Modeling). Replacing PID-MSE with standard MSE ( w/o PID ) also leads to performance degradation in most cases, showing the benefit of feedback-inspired discrepancy modeling. By decomposing prediction errors into proportional, accumulated, and differential components, PID-MSE simultaneously suppresses systematic bias and local oscillations during training. This is particularly beneficial for noisy urban signals, as reflected in the consistent improvements observed for crime and service call prediction. The results suggest that regulating optimization dynamics is as important as improving the fusion strategy itself. Figure 3 . Region Embedding Size Study

sections.heading: 5.4. Parameter Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: Effects of Region Embedding Size. We investigate the impact of region embedding dimensionality on model performance by varying the embedding size from 32 to 288 dimensions. Figure 3 summarizes the MAE and RMSE results. Overall, the performance exhibits a non-monotonic trend as the embedding size increases. Very small embeddings (e.g., 32) tend to underperform, suggesting insufficient representational capacity to capture complex spatial semantics and cross-region interactions. As the dimensionality increases, the performance improves consistently, indicating that richer embeddings encode heterogeneous urban signals better. However, further enlarging the embeddings does not always yield gains. When the dimensionality becomes very large (e.g., 288), the performance either saturates or decreases slightly in several settings. This phenomenon likely stems from over-parameterization, which can introduce redundant features, amplify noise, and increase optimization difficulty. Interestingly, the optimal embedding size remains relatively stable across cities, typically falling within the mid-range (96–144 dimensions). This suggests that urban region representations require sufficient capacity to model functional diversity but also benefit from controlled compactness to preserve generalization. From a task perspective, service call prediction appears more sensitive to embedding dimensionality than crime forecasting, possibly because service demand is influenced by a broader set of socio-economic factors that require richer representations. These findings reveal an important trade-off between representational capacity and model robustness. While larger embeddings enhance expressiveness, overly high dimensionality may harm generalization. The results thus support the use of moderately sized embeddings, which achieve strong predictive performance while also comtributing to computational efficiency. Figure 4 . sections.heading: 5.7. Model Behavior Analysis
sections.text: To understand the mechanisms underlying the performance improvements offered by PRISM , we analyze its behavior from two perspectives: modality heterogeneity and optimization stability. Model Heterogeneity. Figure 7(a) reports the Top-1 routed view ratio across different city–task combinations, thus indicating how frequently each modality is selected as the dominant expert. The results show clear task- and city-specific modality preferences. In NYC, the Land modality consistently dominates across all three tasks, suggesting that land-use information plays a primary role in regional prediction. In Chi , routing decisions appear more balanced, particularly for Crime and Service Call, where POI and Land exhibit comparable selection frequencies, reflecting stronger cross-modal complementarity. In SF, the Crime task is dominated by the Mobility modality, indicating a strong dependence on human mobility patterns. These observations indicate substantial modality heterogeneity across city–task settings. The relative importance of modalities varies markedly depending on both the urban context and the prediction objective. Therefore, a fixed fusion strategy is unlikely to perform optimally across all scenarios. In contrast, the adaptive routing mechanism in PRISM adjusts its modality selection dynamically according to task-specific signals, enabling more context-aware representation learning. (a) Modality heterogeneity. (b) Optimization instability. Figure 7 . Model Behavior Analysis. Optimization Instability. Figure 7(b) examines the optimization dynamics by comparing the training stability of PRISM (PID-MSE) and HAFusion (MSE). Across all city–task combinations, PRISM consistently achieves lower instability scores throughout the training. HAFusion exhibits higher and more fluctuating stability values, indicating stronger gradient imbalance and inter-modal conflicts. The performance gap remains stable across epochs, suggesting that the improvement is due to systematic optimization advantages rather than transient effects. Lower instability scores imply better alignment among modality-specific gradients and reduced scale disparity during joint optimization. By incorporating routing and PID-based regulation, PRISM mitigates gradient competition across modalities and promotes more coordinated multi-view learning. Consequently, the adaptive routing mechanism not only captures heterogeneous modality relevance but also improves optimization stability, thereby explaining the consistent performance gains observed across city–task settings.

To systematically evaluate the robustness of PRISM and HAFusion under these challenging conditions, we perform experiments in missing-view and noisy-view settings. Figure 8 . Performance Across Different Missing View Ratio

sections.heading: 5.8.1. Missing Views.
sections.text: Motivated by the modality heterogeneity analysis in Figure 7(a) , we investigate the robustness of PRISM in different missing-view scenarios. Specifically, we simulate missing views for the dominant modality in each city: we mask the Land view for NYC, the POI view for Chi, and the Mobility view for SF. We vary the missing-view ratio in { 0 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \{0,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0\} , where a ratio of 0 indicates no masking and 1.0 corresponds to complete removal of the selected view. Figure 8 reports the prediction performance findings. As the missing ratio increases, the performance of both methods degrades consistently, confirming the importance of the masked modality. However, PRISM maintains the best performance across nearly all missing ratios and city–task combinations. The performance gap becomes more pronounced under moderate to high missing ratios, indicating that adaptive routing enables the model to better compensate for incomplete information by dynamically reallocating attention to the remaining informative views. Figure 8 also shows that HAFusion slightly outperforms PRISM on SF Crime when the mobility missing ratio is 0.7. This case reveals a limitation of sparse routing under severe dominant-view incompleteness. Since SF Crime relies strongly on mobility-related signals, heavily masking the mobility view can make top- k k routing decisions less reliable. By contrast, the dense fusion strategy in HAFusion aggregates all available views and may provide more stable behavior at this specific corruption level. This result suggests that sparse view selection is generally beneficial, but may require missingness-aware or uncertainty-aware routing when the dominant modality is severely corrupted. Even when the dominant modality is fully removed (ratio = 1.0), PRISM continues to outperform the baseline in most cases. Overall, these results indicate that the routing mechanism enhances resilience to view incompleteness by preventing over-reliance on a single modality and encouraging more balanced multi-view representation learning.

In NYC, performance declines steadily as the corruption ratio increases, with the most pronounced degradation observed in the Crime task; nevertheless, PRISM consistently maintains higher R 2 R^{2} scores than HAFusion , and the performance gap widens under severe noise ( 0.9 0.9 ). In Chicago, both methods exhibit sharper drops compared to NYC, particularly for Crime and Service Call prediction; however, PRISM demonstrates slower performance decay, indicating improved robustness under moderate-to-high corruption levels. For San Francisco, the degradation trend is comparatively smoother across all three tasks, and PRISM preserves a stable margin over the baseline even at the highest noise ratio, suggesting stronger resistance to stochastic perturbations across diverse urban prediction scenarios. Figure 10 presents the results for mixture-of-Gaussians perturbations. In NYC, performance degrades monotonically with increasing corruption, and PRISM achieves competitive performance than the strongest baseline HAFusion across all three tasks. In Chi, both methods decline as noise intensifies; notably, for the Check-in task at ratio 0.1 0.1 , HAFusion slightly surpasses PRISM , whereas PRISM it the best at higher corruption levels. For Crime and Service Call prediction in Chi, PRISM remains consistently better. In SF, degradation is relatively smooth, and PRISM preserves higher R 2 R^{2} scores across all tasks and noise ratios. Column-Wise Shuffle. Figure 11 presents the results for column-wise shuffling, which permutes feature dimensions to disrupt intra-view structural dependencies. In NYC, both methods exhibit nearly identical degradation patterns across Check-in, Crime, and Service Call prediction. Performance decreases consistently as the shuffle ratio increases, while the gap between PRISM and HAFusion remains marginal across all corruption levels. In contrast, for Chi and SF, PRISM consistently achieves higher R 2 R^{2} scores across all three tasks and shuffle ratios. The performance gap becomes more pronounced under moderate-to-high shuffle ratios, particularly for Crime and Service Call prediction, indicating improved stability under severe structural perturbation.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: We present PRISM , a self-adjusting framework for multi-view urban region representation learning. By integrating region-wise sparse routing with PID-inspired discrepancy regulation, PRISM enables adaptive modality allocation and stabilizes multi-objective optimization. Extensive experiments on three large-scale urban datasets across three tasks exhibit consistent performance improvements over state-of-the-art proposals while maintaining comparable model complexity. Our study highlights the importance of adaptive fusion and feedback-aware optimization in heterogeneous urban representation learning, particularly for achieving stable training and preserving model robustness. Overall, the results show that adaptive mechanisms are essential for task-specific urban region representation learning.

Urban region representation learning encodes heterogeneous urban signals—such as mobility flows, points of interest, and land-use patterns—into unified embeddings for downstream tasks, including check-in prediction, crime forecasting, and service demand estimation. Existing approaches rely on globally shared fusion and joint optimization, implicitly assuming uniform modality importance and naturally balanced multi-objective training. However, urban data is inherently heterogeneous. Our empirical analysis reveals two structural issues: (i) modality utility varies markedly across regions, causing static fusion to overemphasize signals from certain modalities; and (ii) heterogeneous objectives exhibit persistent gradient imbalance, causing representational bias and unstable training. We present PRISM , a self-adjusting framework for adaptive multi-view learning. PRISM adapts sparse MoE routing to learn region-specific view allocations, while a PID (Proportional Integral Derivative)-inspired regulation mechanism mitigates gradient conflicts during optimization. Experiments on three large-scale urban datasets show that PRISM achieves competitive performance than strong multi-view baselines, while providing more stable optimization behavior and more balanced region representations. † † authors: . Introduction Cities are increasingly instrumented with sensing and digital infrastructures that continuously generate heterogeneous data from mobility networks, land-use registries, transportation systems, and socio-economic activities ( Xu et al., 2025a ) . This data provides unprecedented opportunities for understanding urban dynamics. Yet, heterogeneity in terms of structure, granularity, noise ratio, and spatial coverage poses fundamental data integration and computational modeling challenges. Urban region representation learning has emerged as a principled abstraction for addressing these challenges ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2027 ) . Transforming diverse urban signals into compact embeddings enables computational models that capture latent spatial functionality and inter-region relationships in a unified vector form. These embeddings serve as reusable, transferable representations that support a wide range of analytical tasks, including check-in prediction ( Liang and Zhang, 2023 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) , crime forecasting ( Butt et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , traffic modeling ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2021b ; Yang et al., 2022a ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2027 ; Yang et al., 2021a ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Yang et al., 2022b ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Yang and Yang, 2020 ) , and service demand estimation ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025a ) . Given the heterogeneous nature of urban data, a central question arises: how should multiple urban signals be integrated to construct reliable region representations? Structured multi-view fusion. Existing approaches treat each urban modality—such as mobility flow graphs, POI distributions, or land-use maps—as an independent structured signal that is encoded using graph or attribute-based models. Representative methods (e.g., MGFN ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , HAFusion ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , CGAP ( Xu and Zhou, 2024 ) ) jointly learn representations from multiple modalities and fuse them by means of concatenation, attention, or weighted aggregation. More recent studies extend this paradigm to cross-modal settings by incorporating additional sources such as street-view images (e.g., FlexiReg ( Sun et al., 2025a ) ). While being architecturally diverse, these methods adopt a shared abstraction: heterogeneous views are integrated via globally shared fusion mechanisms under deterministic parameterization. Multi-objective optimization in multi-view learning. Multi-view urban representation learning typically introduces modality-specific objectives that guide the shared embedding towards distinct structural or semantic properties. These objectives are then jointly optimized within a unified parameter space without explicit coordination. Although general multi-task strategies (e.g., gradient normalization or projection) have been explored in other domains, they assume task symmetry and do not account for the spatially heterogeneous and modality-dependent dynamics intrinsic to urban data. Despite their methodological variations, existing approaches rely on two implicit assumptions: (i) modality importance is spatially consistent across regions , and (ii) joint optimization of heterogeneous objectives naturally produces coordinated and balanced representations . Motivating example. To evaluate these assumptions, we analyze on three city-scale datasets (see Figure 1 ). Figure 1 a highlights task-dependent differences in modality utility: mobility signals are most informative for crime prediction, whereas land-use and POI features are more useful for service call prediction, suggesting differing underlying spatial dynamics. Notably, as highlighted by the red dashed oval, POI and land-use features contribute negligibly to the SF Crime task. This pronounced heterogeneity challenges the assumption of globally uniform fusion across modalities. Figure 1 b further reveals a systematic optimization imbalance under conventional joint training (e.g., the red dashed oval). Gradients associated with different modality-specific objectives exhibit persistent magnitude disparities, allowing dominant modalities to steer the shared embedding space while suppressing weaker yet informative signals. Such imbalance induces representational bias and ultimately degrades cross-region generalization. Figure 1 . Motivation Example on San Francisco Dataset. Following this analysis, we identify two coupled research challenges that remain unresolved in urban region representation learning: Challenge 1 (C1): Spatially adaptive view integration. The predictive utility of each modality is inherently region-dependent, and yet existing fusion mechanisms assign contributions through globally shared parameters. This mismatch between local data characteristics and global fusion strategies incurs representational bias—commercial regions may be well-served while residential regions may be systematically under-represented. The challenge is to enable region-aware, adaptive modality selection that aligns representation capacity with spatial heterogeneity, without requiring region-specific supervision. Challenge 2 (C2): Coordinated optimization under heterogeneous objectives. When multiple modality-specific objectives with different gradient scales, noise levels, and convergence rates are jointly optimized in a shared embedding space, objectives associated with certain modalities may contribute disproportionately large or more stable gradients, causing them to dominate the optimization process and suppress weaker modality signals, which in turn leads to imbalanced representations and unstable training. The challenge is to explicitly regulate the interplay among competing objectives so that all informative modalities contribute proportionally to the final representation. To address the two challenges, we propose PRISM ( P er- R egion I ntegration with S elf-regulating M ulti-view coordination), a unified framework that redefines multi-view urban representation learning as an adaptive coordination problem rather than as a static aggregation procedure. In particular, PRISM builds on an existing multi-view encoding backbone and focuses on two components: region-level sparse view routing and PID-inspired discrepancy regulation. Region-level adaptive routing via sparse MoE. For modeling, PRISM instantiates region-level view allocation with a standard sparse MoE routing design. Our goal is not to introduce a new generic MoE routing operator, but to adapt sparse routing to heterogeneous urban view fusion. Different from token-level MoE routing over homogeneous sequence elements, the routed unit in PRISM is a region-view representation derived from mobility, POI, or land-use signals. The router dynamically selects and prioritizes informative views for each region, enabling localized view specialization while suppressing redundant or noisy signals. This addresses C1 by aligning view contributions with the spatial heterogeneity observed in Figure 1 (a). PID-inspired multi-objective discrepancy regulation. For optimization, PRISM introduces a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer to coordinate heterogeneous view-induced objectives. We borrow the proportional–integral–derivative decomposition to model complementary discrepancy signals during training. Specifically, the proportional term captures the current discrepancy, the integral term captures accumulated bias, and the derivative term captures short-term variation. These terms are used as loss-level regularization penalties rather than as a single control signal acting on the system. This transforms multi-view learning from implicit joint optimization into an explicitly regularized coordination process, addressing the gradient imbalance identified in C2 . In summary, the main contributions are as follows: • Region-Level Adaptive View Allocation. We formulate multi-view urban representation learning as a region-level adaptive view allocation problem, where different regions may rely on different subsets of mobility, POI, and land-use signals. We instantiate this formulation with sparse MoE routing to enable selective view integration at the region granularity. • PID-Inspired Optimization Coordination. We formulate multi-view representation learning as an adaptive optimization coordination problem and introduce a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer that captures current discrepancy, accumulated bias, and local variation. The final loss aggregation adopts uncertainty-based weighting to adaptively balance heterogeneous objectives, while the proposed contribution lies in PID-inspired discrepancy modeling rather than the weighting scheme. This design mitigates gradient conflicts and stabilizes training under heterogeneous view-induced objectives. • Comprehensive Empirical Validation. Extensive experiments on three large-scale urban datasets across multiple downstream tasks evaluate the effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency of PRISM . 2. Related Work 2.1. Urban Region Representation Learning Urban region representation learning aims to derive compact embeddings that encode functional, structural, and interaction patterns of spatial regions. From a data modeling perspective, existing work can be broadly categorized into single-source modeling and heterogeneous multi-source modeling , according to how urban signals are organized and integrated. Single-source approaches learn region embeddings from a dominant urban signal ( Yao et al., 2018 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) , such as mobility flows, POI distributions, or land-use attributes. For example ZE-Mob ( Yao et al., 2018 ) encodes a mobility transition graph using skip-grams. This type of method typically constructs region-level graphs or attribute matrices and apply graph representation learning, random-walk-based embedding, or matrix factorization techniques to obtain compact representations. Some studies extend this paradigm by extracting multiple complementary views from the same modality, e.g., using temporal slicing of mobility flows or structural and semantic similarity graphs, and then aggregate these views, the goal being to enhance robustness ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) . While such designs enrich representations based on a single modality, the learned embeddings remain shaped by the inductive bias and information scope of the specific modality. To increase representational completeness, more recent studies ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023c ; Sun et al., 2025a ) integrate heterogeneous urban signals, including mobility, POIs, land use, socio-economic attributes, and environmental features. These methods seek to capture complementary information from different modalities by constructing multi-graph architectures, cross-attention mechanisms, shared latent spaces, or fusion-based embedding frameworks. Employing joint optimization, they aim to produce unified region representations that reflect multiple aspects of urban dynamics. Modality interactions are typically modeled through feature concatenation or shared attention mechanisms, resulting in a single embedding embodying information from all available views. 2.2. Mixture-of-Experts and Adaptive Routing Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models enable conditional computation by routing inputs to specialized experts through learned gating functions ( Li et al., 2023a ; Nguyen et al., 2024a ) . They have been widely adopted in large-scale neural models to increase model capacity while maintaining computational efficiency ( Nie et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Existing MoE routing strategies mainly differ in sparsity and expert-allocation design. Switch Transformer ( Fedus et al., 2022 ) performs sparse token-level routing by assigning each token to selected feed-forward experts, while GShard ( Lepikhin et al., 2021 ) adopts top- k k routing with auxiliary balancing losses. Expert Choice ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) reverses the assignment direction to improve expert utilization, and Soft MoE ( Puigcerver et al., 2024 ) replaces discrete routing with continuous mixture weights. These methods are primarily developed for homogeneous token streams and emphasize scalability, load balancing, and efficient conditional computation. Recent studies extend MoE to multi-modal and spatio-temporal settings. In multi-modal learning, methods such as MoME ( Shen et al., 2024 ) and VLMo ( Bao et al., 2022 ) activate experts according to modality or layer-level signals. In spatio-temporal forecasting, ST-MoE ( Li et al., 2023b ) routes temporal inputs to specialized experts to capture temporal heterogeneity. MoE has also been explored in urban computing. For example, UrbanMoE ( Liu et al., 2026 ) applies sparse multi-modal expert routing to multi-task urban region profiling, using satellite imagery, textual descriptions, and POI features to predict multiple urban indicators. Different from these studies, PRISM focuses on reusable urban region representation learning from mobility, POI, and land-use views. Its goal is not to introduce a new generic MoE routing operator, but to adapt standard sparse MoE routing to region-level heterogeneous view allocation. In this setting, the routed unit is a region-view representation, and the routing decision determines which urban views should contribute to each region. This differs from token-level routing in large language models, modality-aware routing in multi-modal learning, temporal routing in forecasting, and task-aware expert routing in urban profiling. Recent meta-learning studies further explore spatial adaptation in urban prediction, such as region-adaptive prediction with region profiles and few-shot transfer from data-sufficient cities to data-scarce cities ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) . These methods mainly adapt prediction models under limited observations, whereas PRISM studies region-level coordination among structurally distinct urban views within a unified representation learning framework. 2.3. Adaptive Multi-Task Learning and PID-Inspired Regulation Adaptive multi-task learning (MTL) jointly optimizes multiple objectives while mitigating task imbalance and gradient interference. Representative methods include GradNorm ( Chen et al., 2018 ) , which balances task training rates through gradient magnitude normalization; PCGrad ( Yu et al., 2020 ) , which projects conflicting gradients; and MGDA ( Désidéri, 2012 ; Sener and Koltun, 2018 ) , which seeks a common descent direction toward Pareto-stationary solutions. These methods mainly operate on instantaneous task gradients and are typically designed for conventional MTL settings with comparable supervised tasks. Several recent studies incorporate PID principles into neural learning systems, but at different levels. PIDformer ( Nguyen et al., 2024b ) introduces a PID closed-loop feedback signal into transformer state-space dynamics to improve robustness and mitigate rank collapse. PID-based stochastic optimization ( An et al., 2018 ) treats gradients as control errors and updates network parameters using current, accumulated, and changing gradient information. Different from these methods, PRISM addresses heterogeneous view-induced objectives in urban representation learning, where mobility models origin–destination interactions, while POI and land-use preserve view-specific similarity structures. PRISM does not apply PID to attention dynamics or optimizer states. Instead, it introduces a PID-inspired discrepancy regularizer over view-induced objectives, where the proportional, integral, and derivative terms model current discrepancy, accumulated bias, and short-term variation during training. We further include GradNorm , PCGrad , and MGDA as controlled baselines under the same backbone to empirically examine this distinction. Figure 2 . The PRISM framework.
